misconceptions.say: On `sizeof(int)`: it is 4 on very nearly every machine you will ever meet, and that is still not something the standard promises. What the standard gives you is minimum ranges and an ordering between the types, not fixed widths — which is the entire reason `<cstdint>` exists.

feedback.nudge: Keep two questions apart: what is true on the machine in front of you, and what the standard actually guarantees. Only the second kind belongs in this list.

distractors.0: Guaranteed, and true by definition. `sizeof` counts in units of `char`, so `sizeof(char) == 1` always — on every machine, including ones where a `char` is 16 or 32 bits. Note that this does *not* mean a char is 8 bits: `CHAR_BIT` is at least 8 and is 8 on everything you will meet, but the standard permits more.
distractors.1: Guaranteed. The standard fixes the *ordering*: `char` <= `short` <= `int` <= `long` <= `long long`, along with minimum widths of 8, 16, 16, 32 and 64 bits. So `int` can be the same size as `short`, and on many embedded platforms it is — but it can never be smaller.
distractors.2: Not guaranteed, and this is the one that catches people. `int` is only required to be at least 16 bits. It is 4 bytes on every desktop and server you are likely to use, which is exactly why the assumption is so easy to make and so hard to notice — until you compile for an AVR or an MSP430, where it is 2.
distractors.3: Guaranteed. `sizeof` yields `std::size_t` from `<cstddef>`, an unsigned type big enough to hold the size of any object. Being unsigned matters: `sizeof(int) - sizeof(double)` is not -4 but an enormous positive number, which is the unsigned-wrapping trap in a place nobody expects it.
